items.title: GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com. This has been one of the most requested features in the Desktop community. With this release, you can: Add more than one account for a single host, with no fixed limit. Associate each repository with a specific account, so clone, publish, and Git operations use the right credentials automatically. Choose an account when adding or cloning a repository that multiple signed-in accounts can access, or let Desktop infer it when only one can. Change a repository’s account association at any time from repository settings or the repository list’s context menu. Existing repositories are migrated automatically to the account you were already using, so if you only have one account per host, nothing changes for you. To get started, download the latest (GitHub Desktop 3.7.0) and open Settings/Options > Accounts to add another account, then use the new account picker when cloning, publishing, or reviewing a repository’s settings. Learn more in GitHub Desktop’s authentication documentation. The post GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub Desktop now supports several accounts per host and picks the right credentials per repo. Useful for staff-augmentation engineers who switch between client GitHub accounts.

items.title: Improvements on the pull request overview in public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Your feedback has helped improve the new pull request Overview page since its November 5, 2026 public preview. Here’s what’s new! Clearer merge status and next steps Failed optional checks no longer make mergeable pull requests appear blocked. Previously missing merge requirements now show what needs attention. Readiness summary gives reviewers and visitors clearer guidance, including when no action is needed. Smoother review and comment interactions Checks and approvals now expand when clicked, instead of pinning a preview. Fixed overlapping previews and mobile interaction issues. Resolved review threads now collapse to keep completed conversations out of the way. Comments mentioning Copilot now better explain the action and selected model before submission. Activity details Force-push activity now links to the old and new commits so you can compare changes. Commit activity now includes timestamps so you can see when changes were made. Page layout and sidebar actions Source and target branches now stay visible on smaller screens. Edit links in the Development sidebar directly in Overview. Lock or unlock PR conversations directly in Overview. Fixed uneven spacing, misalignment, and sidebar gaps across screen sizes. Try the new overview page and give feedback To join, select the ✨ Try the Overview page button in the header. You can use the same menu to return to the classic overview during the preview. This preview is very much a starting point, not the finished pull request experience. Try it on your next pull request. What is easier to find? Where do you still lose context? What sends you back to the classic overview? Share your feedback and report issues in the overview preview feedback discussion. The post Improvements on the pull request overview in public preview appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: The GitHub PR overview preview now shows merge status more clearly, and failed optional checks no longer make a PR look blocked. Small quality-of-life gains for our review pipelines.

items.title: GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23 release candidate
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.23 is now available and introduces new capabilities across the platform. Here are a few highlights in the 3.23 release: When working in GitHub Projects, you can create more precise project views by combining filters with logical OR, explicit AND, and parentheses for grouping. For example, (status:Done OR status:Todo) is:issue shows issues with either status. If your enterprise uses GitHub Secret Protection, you can detect unstructured secrets entirely within your network using AI secret detection on GHES, including in air-gapped environments. A self-contained, fine-tuned model runs on the appliance’s CPU without a GPU, hosted LLM, or outbound connection. This feature is in public preview and subject to change. As a developer, you can identify known malicious packages in PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, Rust, and Composer through the GitHub Advisory Database, in addition to npm. The database automatically ingests malware advisories from OpenSSF’s malicious-packages repository to expand coverage across these ecosystems. By default, Dependabot waits until a package version has been available on its registry for at least three days before opening a version update pull request. This cooldown gives maintainers and the community more time to detect and report compromised or buggy releases before users merge updates. As an OAuth app developer, you can limit token lifetimes by using access tokens that expire after eight hours and refresh tokens to obtain new access tokens. Token expiration is opt-in for existing OAuth apps and the default for newly created apps. You can request expiring tokens with scope=offline_access during authorization for testing and gradual rollout, or require expiration in your app registration. Before requiring expiration, you must update all clients to request, store, and use refresh tokens to avoid breaking sign-in for clients that do not support them. This feature is in public preview and subject to change. In yo
items.why_it_matters: Release candidate for self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23, with AI secret detection and better project filters. It mostly matters for enterprise clients that run GHES.

items.title: Security advisory permissions are now generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles. You no longer have to make them repository administrators or give them the organization-wide security manager role. Four new permissions are available under Security when you create or edit a custom repository role: View security advisories: view draft security advisories, their status, and comments. Create, Edit, and Manage security advisories: everything in View, plus Create and Edit advisories, comment, manage collaborators, and create a temporary private fork. Accept private vulnerability reports and close or reopen security advisories: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Publish security advisories and request CVEs: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Assign the role to users and teams on only the repositories where they need it. The permissions apply to both repository security advisories and private vulnerability reports, so you can give a team access to the repositories they maintain without exposing advisories across your whole organization. A few things to know: Merging changes from a temporary private fork still requires a repository administrator or security manager. People with any of these new permissions can’t delete a temporary private fork. Confidential comments are only available to people with Create, Edit, and Manage who also have write access to the repository. This is available to organizations on plans that support custom repository roles, including GitHub Enterprise Cloud. To get started, see Repository security advisories in the GitHub Docs. The post Security advisory permissions are now generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Custom GitHub repo roles can now handle security advisories and private vulnerability reports without admin rights. This is useful least-privilege setup for client repos.

items.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.excerpt: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems, which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems, there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic, Theorem, Axiom Math, and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett, &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5, a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro, Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existin
items.why_it_matters: Covers formal verification as a way to check AI-generated code, and the startups offering it. This fits our verification-over-vibes approach, though near-term use in web stacks is limited.

items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.excerpt: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation. We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.excerpt: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube, ai, generative-ai, llms, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai-misuse
items.why_it_matters: Groups are abusing free trials of AI products to get free tokens and resell them. This matters to anyone building LLM features into client MVPs: plan for abuse prevention, rate limits and cost controls from the start.
